yes_case.case: The closest historical episodes are the dramatic H-1B fee increases and regulatory overhaul attempts during the first Trump administration, specifically the October 2020 Interim Final Rule that attempted to drastically alter wage-level selections, and the October 2020 Department of Labor rule that substantially raised prevailing wage requirements to price out foreign workers. This episode differs fundamentally because the proposed $103,265 fee is an order of magnitude larger than past adjustments, transforming the H-1B program from a skilled-worker pipeline into an ultra-luxury tier. Unlike the 2020 attempts which relied on complex wage-level tier manipulations that invited technical judicial challenges, this episode utilizes a blunt, massive absolute fee figure designed to test the absolute outer limits of executive statutory authority under the Immigration and Nationality Act. Furthermore, while past episodes were executed late in an administration under severe time constraints, a 2027 target date provides an unprecedented multi-year runway to refine the economic justification and insulate the rulemaking from the procedural vulnerabilities that sank the 2020 initiatives.
key_evidence: The October 2020 DHS Interim Final Rule on H-1B wage levels
The October 2020 Department of Labor interim final rule on prevailing wages
The targeted $103,265 fee magnitude which shifts the policy mechanism from wage restructuring to prohibitive taxation
yes_case.strength_reason: Historical precedent shows a clear executive appetite for using severe economic barriers to restrict H-1B usage, but the unprecedented scale of the $103,265 figure creates a novel legal and economic paradigm compared to past episodes.
yes_case.deliberately_ignored: I left aside all analysis of procedural steps, Federal Register publication schedules, notice-and-comment timelines, administrative law mechanics, court injunction probabilities, and population-level statistical impacts on visa applicants.

no_case.case: The closest historical episodes are the extreme H-1B fee hike proposals from the late 2017-2020 Trump administration, such as the Department of Labor's 2020 interim final rule drastically inflating prevailing wage tiers, and the 2020 DHS rule attempting to fundamentally restructure H-1B selections through salary-ranking. This current episode differs crucially because the magnitude of the $103,265 figure represents an unprecedented three-orders-of-magnitude increase over historical baseline fees rather than a marginal or percentage-based adjustment. Past episodes involved incremental regulatory levers that, while aggressive, operated within established statutory bounds of 'reasonable cost recovery' and economic adjustments. A six-figure fee for a standard employment visa lacks any historical precedent in U.S. immigration rulemaking, making it fundamentally distinct from previous policy vehicles. Because past attempts at aggressive structural overhaul were invariably tied to complex administrative justifications that still foundered on standard APA arbitrary-and-capricious hurdles, this extreme outlier lacks even the plausible regulatory scaffolding of its predecessors, ensuring it will fail to clear the final rule threshold before the August 2027 deadline.
key_evidence: The 2020 Department of Labor interim final rule on prevailing wages

no_case.strength_reason: The historical record shows that past executive actions attempting sweeping H-1B reforms relied on tethering changes to wage data or operational definitions, whereas a rigid $103,265 fee is an unprecedented astronomical leap that severs the policy from any past analog of successful rulemaking.

yes_case.case: The structural apparatus of the executive branch possesses overwhelming unilateral authority to promulgate administrative fees through the notice-and-comment rulemaking process under the APA, provided procedural boxes are checked. In the domain of immigration fee restructuring, external structural friction is limited to Administrative Procedure Act (APA) challenges and procedural injunctions. Historical friction of this kind rarely prevents a determined agency from ultimately curing procedural defects and finalizing a rule; courts routinely remand rules rather than permanently enjoining them, or appellate review lifts preliminary injunctions before statutory deadlines. The structural machinery of regulatory finalization—Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) review, Federal Register publication, and administrative record compilation—is designed to succeed absent permanent statutory prohibition or explicit legislative override, neither of which stands in the path of executive fee-setting authority under current statutory delegations.
